subject: maths
title: Properties of quadrilaterals
summary: Using the side, angle and diagonal properties of special quadrilaterals to find unknown angles, and deciding which properties prove a shape is a parallelogram.
body:
Builders check that a new frame is a true rectangle by measuring its two diagonals: if they are equal, the corners are square. That works because every special quadrilateral has its own set of properties — about sides, angles and diagonals — and knowing them lets you find hidden angles and prove what a shape really is.

## Learning objective

By the end of this lesson you can use the properties of special quadrilaterals, especially their diagonals, to find unknown angles with reasons, and decide which properties are enough to prove a shape is a parallelogram.

## Before you start

You need Quadrilaterals (Year 7), Angles and parallel lines and Angle sums of triangles (Year 8).

**Warm-up**

1. A quadrilateral has angles 85°, 95° and 100°. Find the fourth angle.
2. One angle of a parallelogram is 58°. Find the angle next to it.

*Answers:* 1. 80° 2. 122°

## Think of it like this

### Family members and their traits

Think of the special quadrilaterals as a family. The **parallelogram** is the parent. The rectangle inherits everything from the parent and adds "all angles 90°". The rhombus inherits everything and adds "all sides equal". The square inherits from both, so it has every trait. If you know a shape's family tree, you know all its traits for free.

*Where the analogy breaks down:* the kite and the trapezium are not children of the parallelogram — they are more like cousins with their own separate traits.

## Key ideas

### Diagonal properties

A **diagonal** joins two opposite corners. **Bisect** means cut into two equal parts.

| Shape | Diagonals bisect each other | Diagonals equal | Diagonals at 90° | Diagonals bisect the corner angles |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parallelogram | yes | no | no | no |
| Rectangle | yes | yes | no | no |
| Rhombus | yes | no | yes | yes |
| Square | yes | yes | yes | yes (into 45°) |
| Kite | one diagonal cuts the other in half | no | yes | one diagonal bisects two angles |

### Diagonals make triangles you already know

This is where the angle rules come from.

- **Rectangle:** the diagonals are equal and cut each other in half, so the four half-diagonals are all the same length. Each of the four triangles where the diagonals cross is **isosceles**.

![Rectangle ABCD with diagonals AC and BD meeting at O. All four half-diagonals OA, OB, OC and OD have the same tick mark](/diagrams/y8/maths/properties-of-quadrilaterals-rect.svg)
- **Rhombus:** the diagonals cross at 90° and cut each corner angle in half, so the four triangles are **right-angled** and identical.

![Rhombus PQRS with all four sides marked equal. The diagonals PR and QS cross at O at a right angle. At Q the diagonal splits the corner angle into two equal angles, each labelled y](/diagrams/y8/maths/properties-of-quadrilaterals-rhombus.svg)
- **Kite:** the main diagonal (the one joining the corners between the equal sides) is a line of symmetry. It cuts those two corner angles in half and crosses the other diagonal at 90°.

### Trapeziums

In a **trapezium** (one pair of parallel sides), the two angles along each slanted side are co-interior, so they add to 180°. An **isosceles trapezium** has its two slanted sides equal. Its angles at each end of a parallel side are equal (the **base angles**), and its diagonals are equal.

### Proving a shape is a parallelogram

A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if you can show **any one** of these:

- both pairs of opposite sides are parallel;
- both pairs of opposite sides are equal;
- both pairs of opposite angles are equal;
- the diagonals bisect each other;
- one pair of sides is both equal and parallel.

Be careful with half-facts: equal diagonals alone, or diagonals at 90° alone, do **not** prove any special shape — a kite has diagonals at 90° and an isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals.

## Worked examples

### Example 1

Rectangle ABCD has diagonals that meet at O. ∠OAB = 35°. Find ∠AOB.

![Rectangle ABCD with diagonals meeting at O. Angle OAB is 35° and angle AOB is marked with a question mark](/diagrams/y8/maths/properties-of-quadrilaterals-ex1.svg)

Step 1: OA = OB — the diagonals of a rectangle are equal and bisect each other.
Step 2: Triangle AOB is isosceles, so ∠OBA = ∠OAB = 35°.
Step 3: ∠AOB = 180 − 35 − 35 = 110° — angle sum of a triangle.

### Example 2

Rhombus PQRS has ∠PQR = 130°. Its diagonals meet at O. Find ∠QPO.

![Rhombus PQRS with diagonals meeting at O at a right angle. Angle PQR is 130° and angle QPO is marked with a question mark](/diagrams/y8/maths/properties-of-quadrilaterals-ex2.svg)

Step 1: Diagonal QS bisects ∠PQR, so ∠PQO = 130 ÷ 2 = 65°.
Step 2: The diagonals of a rhombus cross at 90°, so ∠POQ = 90°.
Step 3: In triangle POQ, ∠QPO = 180 − 90 − 65 = 25°.
Check: ∠QPS = 180 − 130 = 50° (co-interior), and diagonal PR halves it: 25° ✓

### Example 3

In a kite, the two equal angles are opposite each other. The other two angles are 70° and 50°. Find each equal angle.

Step 1: The angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°.
Step 2: The two equal angles together are 360 − 70 − 50 = 240°.
Step 3: Each equal angle is 240 ÷ 2 = 120°.
Check: 120 + 120 + 70 + 50 = 360 ✓

### Example 4

In parallelogram ABCD, opposite angles are ∠A = (3x + 10)° and ∠C = (5x − 30)°. Find ∠B.

Step 1: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal: 3x + 10 = 5x − 30.
Step 2: Subtract 3x and add 30 to both sides: 40 = 2x, so x = 20.
Step 3: ∠A = 3 × 20 + 10 = 70°.
Step 4: ∠B is next to ∠A, so they are co-interior: ∠B = 180 − 70 = 110°.
Check: 70 + 110 + 70 + 110 = 360 ✓

## Common mistakes

- **Giving every shape every diagonal property.** Only rhombuses, squares and kites have diagonals at 90°; only rectangles, squares and isosceles trapeziums have equal diagonals. Fix: check the table.
- **Halving the wrong angle.** In a rhombus the diagonal halves the corner angle, not the angle where the diagonals cross (that is always 90°). Fix: mark the 90° first.
- **Assuming a shape from how it looks.** A shape that looks like a rectangle might not have right angles. Fix: only use properties you are told or have proved.
- **Thinking one property proves a parallelogram.** Equal diagonals alone don't. Fix: use one of the five tests in the list.

## Tips to remember

- **The family tree:** parallelogram → rectangle (adds right angles) and rhombus (adds equal sides) → square (has both). Children inherit all the parent's properties.
- **"Rhombus = right-angle cross":** rhombus diagonals cross at 90° and halve the corners. (Made-up memory trick.)
- **"Rectangle = equal diagonals = isosceles triangles":** the crossing point is the same distance from all four corners. (Made-up memory trick.)
- **Trapezium sides:** along each slanted side, the two angles add to 180° — it's the C shape again.
- **Self-check:** your four angles must add to 360°.

## Key terms

- **Diagonal** — a line joining two opposite corners of a polygon.
- **Bisect** — cut into two equal parts.
- **Isosceles trapezium** — a trapezium whose two non-parallel sides are equal; its base angles and diagonals are equal.
- **Axis of symmetry** — a line that cuts a shape into two mirror-image halves.
- **Property** — a fact that is true for every shape of that type.

## Summary

- Parallelogram diagonals bisect each other; rectangles add equal diagonals; rhombuses add diagonals at 90° that halve the corners.
- Diagonals split shapes into triangles: isosceles in a rectangle, right-angled in a rhombus.
- A kite's main diagonal is a line of symmetry and meets the other diagonal at 90°.
- Angles along a trapezium's slanted side add to 180°.
- A quadrilateral is a parallelogram if its diagonals bisect each other, or its opposite sides are equal, or its opposite angles are equal, or its opposite sides are parallel, or one pair of sides is equal and parallel.

questions.prompt: Which property is true for every rhombus but NOT for every parallelogram?

options.C: The diagonals cross at right angles
options.D: The diagonals are equal in length

questions.explanation: Rhombus diagonals always cross at 90°, but a general parallelogram's diagonals do not. Parallel opposite sides and equal opposite angles are true for every parallelogram, so they don't single out the rhombus.
steps: A rhombus is a parallelogram with all sides equal, so it has every parallelogram property plus extra ones.
The extra diagonal properties of a rhombus are: diagonals cross at 90° and halve the corner angles.
So the answer is the diagonals crossing at right angles.

mistakes.A: Step 1: every parallelogram has parallel opposite sides, so this isn't special to the rhombus.
mistakes.B: Step 1: every parallelogram has equal opposite angles, so this isn't special to the rhombus.
mistakes.D: Step 2: equal diagonals belong to rectangles and squares, not to every rhombus.

questions.prompt: ABCD is a trapezium with AB ∥ DC. ∠DAB = 74°. Find ∠ADC.
questions.explanation: ∠DAB and ∠ADC lie along the slanted side AD between the parallel sides, so they are co-interior and add to 180°: 180 − 74 = 106°. 74° is wrong because co-interior angles are not equal.
steps: AB ∥ DC, and AD is a transversal between them.
∠DAB and ∠ADC are co-interior angles, so they add to 180°.

mistakes.B: Step 2: co-interior angles add to 180° — they are not equal.
mistakes.C: Step 2: co-interior angles add to 180°, not 90°.
mistakes.D: Step 2: subtract from 180° (two angles along one side), not 360°.

questions.prompt: Rectangle ABCD has diagonals that meet at O. ∠OBA = 28°. Find ∠AOB.
questions.explanation: OA = OB because rectangle diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so ∠OAB = 28° too and ∠AOB = 180 − 56 = 124°. 152° only subtracts one of the two 28° angles.
steps: Rectangle diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so OA = OB.
Triangle AOB is isosceles, so ∠OAB = ∠OBA = 28°.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 28° is each base angle. Use the angle sum to find the angle at O.
mistakes.B: Step 2: there are two 28° angles in triangle AOB. Subtract both from 180°.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 62° is 90 − 28. ∠AOB is in triangle AOB, so use 180 − 28 − 28.

questions.diagram_alt: Rectangle ABCD with diagonals meeting at O. Angle OBA is 28° and angle AOB is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: Rhombus ABCD has ∠ABC = 110°. Its diagonals meet at O. Find ∠OAB.
questions.explanation: Diagonal BD halves ∠ABC, so ∠OBA = 55°, and the diagonals cross at 90°, so ∠OAB = 180 − 90 − 55 = 35°. 55° is the angle at B, not at A.
steps: Diagonal BD bisects ∠ABC: ∠OBA = 110 ÷ 2 = 55°.
Rhombus diagonals cross at 90°, so ∠AOB = 90°.
In triangle AOB: ∠OAB = 180 − 90 − 55 = 35°.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 55° is ∠OBA, the half-angle at B. You need the angle at A.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 70° is the whole of ∠DAB (180 − 110). Diagonal AC cuts it in half.
mistakes.D: Step 2: the angle at O is 90°. Include it in the angle sum: 180 − 90 − 55.

questions.prompt: A kite has two equal opposite angles of 105° each. One of its other angles is 60°. Find the fourth angle.
questions.explanation: The four angles add to 360°: 360 − 105 − 105 − 60 = 90°. 195° only subtracts one of the 105° angles.
steps: The angles of a quadrilateral add to 360°.
Known angles: 105 + 105 + 60 = 270.
Fourth angle = 360 − 270 = 90°.

mistakes.A: Step 1: in a kite only one pair of opposite angles is equal. Use the angle sum for the fourth angle.
mistakes.B: Step 2: there are two angles of 105°. Add both before subtracting from 360.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 75° is 180 − 105. A quadrilateral's angles add to 360°, not 180°.

questions.prompt: In parallelogram ABCD, the opposite angles ∠A and ∠C are (3x + 12)° and (5x − 28)°. Find ∠B.
questions.explanation: Opposite angles are equal: 3x + 12 = 5x − 28, so x = 20 and ∠A = 72°. ∠B is co-interior with ∠A, so ∠B = 180 − 72 = 108°. 72° is ∠A, not ∠B.
steps: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal: 3x + 12 = 5x − 28.
Subtract 3x and add 28 to both sides: 40 = 2x, so x = 20.
∠B is next to ∠A (co-interior), so ∠B = 180 − 72 = 108°.

mistakes.B: Step 4: 72° is ∠A. ∠B is the angle next to it, so subtract from 180°.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 20 is x. Substitute it to find ∠A, then ∠B.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 40 = 2x, so 40 is 2x, not an angle. Divide by 2 to get x, then find ∠A and ∠B.

questions.prompt: Rectangle ABCD has diagonals that meet at O. ∠AOB = 64°. Find ∠OBC.
questions.explanation: OA = OB, so ∠OBA = (180 − 64) ÷ 2 = 58°. ∠ABC = 90°, so ∠OBC = 90 − 58 = 32°. 58° is ∠OBA, the other part of the right angle.
steps: Rectangle diagonals are equal and bisect each other, so OA = OB and triangle AOB is isosceles.
∠ABC = 90° (rectangle), so ∠OBC = 90 − 58 = 32°.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 58° is ∠OBA. Subtract it from the 90° corner to get ∠OBC.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 90 − 64 uses the angle at O directly. First find ∠OBA from isosceles triangle AOB.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 116° is both base angles together. Halve it, then subtract from 90°.

questions.diagram_alt: Rectangle ABCD with diagonals meeting at O. Angle AOB is 64° and angle OBC is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: ABCD is an isosceles trapezium with AB ∥ DC and AD = BC. ∠DAB = 115°. Find ∠BCD.
questions.explanation: In an isosceles trapezium the base angles are equal, so ∠ABC = 115°. ∠BCD is co-interior with ∠ABC along side BC: 180 − 115 = 65°. 130° is what's left of 360° after the two 115° angles, but it still has to be shared between two angles.
steps: Isosceles trapezium: the angles at each end of AB are equal, so ∠ABC = 115°.
∠ABC and ∠BCD lie along slanted side BC between parallel sides, so they are co-interior.

mistakes.A: Step 2: ∠BCD is at the other parallel side. It's co-interior with ∠ABC, so they add to 180°.
mistakes.C: Step 3: don't halve 115°. ∠BCD and ∠ABC are co-interior, so subtract 115 from 180.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 360 − 115 − 115 = 130 is the total of ∠C and ∠D. Halve it, or use co-interior angles.

questions.diagram_alt: Isosceles trapezium ABCD with AB parallel to DC and AD = BC. Angle DAB is 115° and angle BCD is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: ABCD is a kite with AB = AD and CB = CD. ∠BAD = 70° and ∠ABC = 120°. Diagonal AC is drawn. Find ∠ACB.
questions.explanation: ∠ADC = ∠ABC = 120°, so ∠BCD = 360 − 70 − 240 = 50°. Diagonal AC is the line of symmetry, so it halves ∠BCD: ∠ACB = 25°. 50° is the whole of ∠BCD.
steps: The kite's equal angles are at B and D, so ∠ADC = 120°.
∠BCD = 360 − 70 − 120 − 120 = 50° — angle sum of a quadrilateral.
Diagonal AC is the line of symmetry, so it halves ∠BCD: ∠ACB = 50 ÷ 2 = 25°.

mistakes.B: Step 3: 50° is the whole angle at C. The diagonal AC cuts it in half.
mistakes.C: Step 3: 35° is ∠BAC (half of 70°), the angle at A, not at C.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 60° is half of ∠ABC. The diagonal AC halves the angle at C, not at B.

options.A: A quadrilateral with equal diagonals is a rectangle
options.B: A quadrilateral with diagonals that cross at right angles is a rhombus
options.C: A quadrilateral with one pair of parallel sides and one pair of equal sides is a parallelogram
options.D: A quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other is a parallelogram

questions.explanation: Diagonals that bisect each other is one of the tests for a parallelogram. The others fail: an isosceles trapezium has equal diagonals but isn't a rectangle, and a kite has diagonals at 90° but isn't a rhombus.
steps: Look for a counter-example (a shape that breaks the rule) for each statement.
Isosceles trapezium: equal diagonals, and one pair of parallel sides with the other pair equal — but it's not a rectangle or a parallelogram. Kite: diagonals at 90°, but not a rhombus.
Only 'diagonals bisect each other' has no counter-example — it's a parallelogram test.

mistakes.A: Step 2: an isosceles trapezium also has equal diagonals, and it isn't a rectangle.
mistakes.B: Step 2: a kite's diagonals also cross at 90°, and it isn't a rhombus.
mistakes.C: Step 2: an isosceles trapezium has one pair of parallel sides and one pair of equal sides, but it isn't a parallelogram.

questions.prompt: ABCD is a square. Point E is inside the square so that triangle ABE is equilateral. Find ∠AED.
questions.explanation: AE = AB = AD, so triangle ADE is isosceles. ∠DAE = 90 − 60 = 30°, so ∠AED = (180 − 30) ÷ 2 = 75°. 30° is ∠DAE, the apex angle, not a base angle.
steps: AE = AB (equilateral triangle) and AB = AD (square), so AE = AD and triangle ADE is isosceles.
The base angles of triangle ADE are equal: ∠AED = (180 − 30) ÷ 2 = 75°.

mistakes.A: Step 3: 30° is the apex angle ∠DAE. You need a base angle of triangle ADE.
mistakes.B: Step 2: 60° is an angle of the equilateral triangle. ∠AED is in triangle ADE.
mistakes.D: Step 3: 150° is both base angles together. Halve it.

questions.diagram_alt: Square ABCD with point E inside so that AB, AE and BE are marked equal (equilateral triangle ABE). Segment DE is drawn and angle AED is marked with a question mark

questions.prompt: ABCD is a parallelogram with ∠ADC = 110°. The line that cuts ∠DAB exactly in half meets side DC at E. Find ∠AED.
questions.explanation: ∠DAB = 180 − 110 = 70°, so ∠DAE = 35°. In triangle ADE, ∠AED = 180 − 110 − 35 = 35° (it also equals ∠EAB, alternate angles with AB ∥ DC). 70° forgets to halve ∠DAB.
steps: ∠DAB and ∠ADC are co-interior (AB ∥ DC), so ∠DAB = 180 − 110 = 70°.
AE cuts ∠DAB in half, so ∠DAE = 35°.
Angle sum of triangle ADE: ∠AED = 180 − 110 − 35 = 35°.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 70° is the whole of ∠DAB. The line AE cuts it in half.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 55° is half of 110°. It's ∠DAB (70°) that is cut in half, not ∠ADC.
mistakes.D: Step 3: there are two known angles in triangle ADE (110° and 35°). Subtract both from 180°.
